explanation: The hypothesis directly addresses a credible governing mechanism for hardness and strength in concentrated alloys, and the cited paper supports the proposed link between local chemical order, a rugged dislocation-energy landscape, and increased lattice friction. It is therefore a scientifically plausible alternative rather than a reconstruction of the target, which concerns high-energy ball milling and spark-plasma sintering of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi, nanocrystalline Hall–Petch/dislocation/solid-solution strengthening, and an FCC/BCC phase mixture. The proposed annealed-versus-quenched comparison is testable, includes a baseline, boundaries, predicted mechanical and microscopy observations, and a falsification criterion. Its discriminability is limited because annealing and quenching can also alter grain size, residual stress, vacancy content, segregation, phase fractions, and precipitation; merely requiring similar grain size does not isolate LCO. Demonstrating LCO by conventional XRD or atom-probe composition maps is also nontrivial and would require quantitative short-range-order analysis, ideally supplemented by diffuse scattering or validated atomistic/statistical methods. The evidence is mechanistically relevant but is primarily simulation-based and does not by itself establish that the proposed heat treatment will produce a mechanically measurable strengthening increment without confounding structural changes. No target-specific processing conditions or quantitative outcomes are recovered.
